sourceAlignment.text: Kenneth A. Ross, Elementary Analysis, 2nd edition
sourceAlignment.policy: Original Proof Anvil presentation; no textbook exercise wording or answer sequence is reproduced.

problems.title: Classic tangent cancellation
problems.objective: Evaluate a standard third-order trigonometric cancellation limit with justified repeated differentiation.
problems.statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-x}{x^3}$ using L'Hospital's rule. State the indeterminate form after each application.
permittedResults: Standard derivatives of $\tan x$ and the identity $\sec^2x-1=\tan^2x$.
problems.strategy: Differentiate until the cancellation disappears, checking that every intermediate quotient remains zero-over-zero before applying the rule again.
hints: The second derivative numerator is $2\tan x\sec^2x$.
problems.solution: The original quotient is $0/0$. Three justified applications of L'Hospital's rule give $$\frac{\sec^2x-1}{3x^2}=\frac{\tan^2x}{3x^2},\qquad \frac{2\tan x\sec^2x}{6x},$$ and then $$\frac{2\sec^4x+4\tan^2x\sec^2x}{6}.$$ The first two displayed derivative quotients are still $0/0$, and each denominator derivative is nonzero on a punctured neighborhood of zero. Substitution in the final quotient gives $2/6=1/3$.
rubricCriteria: Records the successive zero-over-zero forms.
Differentiates $\tan x$ and $\tan x\sec^2x$ correctly.
Concludes that the limit is $1/3$.

commonErrors.description: Stops after the first application at another zero-over-zero quotient.
commonErrors.consequence: The limit remains unevaluated.

commonErrors.description: Uses $(\tan x)'=\tan^2x$.
commonErrors.consequence: The repeated derivative calculation is wrong.

problems.flawedProof: Since both $\tan x$ and $x$ have derivative one at zero, their difference has limit zero and the quotient is zero.
problems.leanDraft:
import Mathlib

example (x : ℝ) (hc : Real.cos x ≠ 0) : 1 / Real.cos x ^ 2 - 1 = Real.tan x ^ 2 := by
  rw [Real.tan_eq_sin_div_cos]
  field_simp
  nlinarith [Real.sin_sq_add_cos_sq x]

problems.title: Classic cosine cancellation
problems.objective: Evaluate the fundamental cosine-over-quadratic limit and audit both L'Hospital applications.
permittedResults: Standard derivatives of sine and cosine.
problems.strategy: Apply the rule twice, because the first derivative quotient still has the form zero over zero.
hints: After one application, the quotient is $\sin x/(2x)$.
The second derivative quotient is $\cos x/2$.
problems.solution: Both numerator and denominator tend to zero, and $(x^2)'=2x$ is nonzero for $x\ne0$. L'Hospital's rule gives $\lim_{x\to0}\sin x/(2x)$, which is again $0/0$. Since the next denominator derivative is $2$, a second application gives $$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\cos x}{2}=\frac12.$$
rubricCriteria: Identifies both zero-over-zero forms.
Applies the rule twice with correct derivatives.
Obtains the value $1/2$.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $1-\cos x$ as $-\sin x$.
commonErrors.consequence: The answer has the wrong sign.

commonErrors.description: Stops after obtaining $\sin x/(2x)$.
commonErrors.consequence: A remaining indeterminate quotient is not evaluated.

problems.flawedProof: Substituting zero gives $0/0$, and by cancelling the zeros the answer is one.

  convert (hasDerivAt_const x 1).sub (Real.hasDerivAt_cos x) using 1 <;> ring

problems.title: Exponential growth defeats a fourth power
problems.objective: Use repeated L'Hospital applications to prove a standard polynomial-versus-exponential growth comparison.
problems.statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^4}{e^x}$ using L'Hospital's rule, and explain why the process stops after four applications.
problems.strategy: Differentiate numerator and denominator four times; the polynomial eventually becomes a constant while the exponential is unchanged.
hints: Each of the first four quotients has denominator $e^x$.
A constant divided by $e^x$ tends to zero.
problems.solution: The original quotient has form $\infty/\infty$, and the denominator derivative $e^x$ never vanishes. Repeated applications of L'Hospital's rule give $$\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{x^4}{e^x}=\lim\frac{4x^3}{e^x}=\lim\frac{12x^2}{e^x}=\lim\frac{24x}{e^x}=\lim\frac{24}{e^x}=0.$$ The process stops because the fourth derivative of $x^4$ is constant, so the remaining limit is no longer indeterminate.
rubricCriteria: Verifies the initial infinity-over-infinity form.
Tracks all four numerator derivatives correctly.
Stops when the quotient is no longer indeterminate and concludes zero.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates the quotient using the quotient rule.
commonErrors.consequence: That is not how L'Hospital's replacement quotient is formed.

commonErrors.description: Continues differentiating after reaching $24/e^x$ without evaluating it.
commonErrors.consequence: The stopping criterion for the rule is misunderstood.

problems.flawedProof: Exponentials always beat polynomials, so no calculation or theorem hypotheses are needed.

problems.title: The standard one-to-infinity limit
problems.objective: Use logarithms and L'Hospital's rule to evaluate a canonical one-to-infinity form.
permittedResults: L'Hospital's rule and the derivative of the logarithm.
problems.strategy: Take logarithms, rewrite the exponentiated logarithm as a zero-over-zero quotient, then exponentiate its limit.
problems.solution: For large positive $x$, set $y_x=(1+4/x)^x$. Then $$\log y_x=\frac{\log(1+4/x)}{1/x},$$ a $0/0$ form. L'Hospital's rule gives $$\lim_{x\to\infty}\log y_x=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{-4/[x(x+4)]}{-1/x^2}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{4x}{x+4}=4.$$ Continuity of the exponential yields $y_x\to e^4$.
rubricCriteria: Introduces the logarithm and verifies a positive base.
Computes and simplifies the derivative quotient correctly.
Exponentiates the logarithmic limit to obtain $e^4$.

commonErrors.description: Treats $1^\infty$ as the ordinary value one.
commonErrors.consequence: The indeterminate power is not resolved.

commonErrors.description: Reports four instead of $e^4$.
commonErrors.consequence: The logarithmic limit is confused with the original limit.

problems.flawedProof: The base approaches one, so the power approaches one.

  field_simp
  ring

problems.title: The standard infinity-to-zero power
problems.objective: Evaluate the canonical $\infty^0$ form by logarithmic transformation.
permittedResults: L'Hospital's rule and continuity of the exponential.
problems.strategy: Take logarithms, apply L'Hospital's rule to $\log x/x$, then exponentiate.
hints: The expression has the indeterminate form $\infty^0$.
Its logarithm is $\log x/x$, an $\infty/\infty$ quotient.
problems.solution: For $x>0$, write $x^{1/x}=\exp((\log x)/x)$. The logarithmic quotient has form $\infty/\infty$, so L'Hospital's rule gives $$\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\log x}{x}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1/x}{1}=0.$$ Therefore continuity of the exponential gives $x^{1/x}\to e^0=1$.
rubricCriteria: Recognizes the infinity-to-zero form and takes logarithms.
Applies L'Hospital's rule to the logarithmic quotient.
Returns from the logarithm and obtains one.

commonErrors.description: Declares $\infty^0=1$ by exponent rules.
commonErrors.consequence: An indeterminate form is treated as ordinary arithmetic.

commonErrors.description: Finds the logarithmic limit zero but reports zero.
commonErrors.consequence: The final exponential transformation is omitted.

problems.flawedProof: Any positive number raised to the zeroth power is one, so the limit is one.

problems.title: A power times a logarithm
problems.objective: Resolve a standard zero-times-infinity form by converting it to an infinite quotient.
problems.strategy: Rewrite the product as $\log x/x^{-2}$ and differentiate numerator and denominator.
hints: The product has form $0\cdot(-\infty)$, not a quotient yet.
problems.solution: Rewrite $$x^2\log x=\frac{\log x}{x^{-2}}.$$ As $x\to0^+$, the numerator tends to $-\infty$ and the denominator to $+\infty$. The denominator derivative $-2x^{-3}$ is nonzero for $x>0$, so L'Hospital's rule gives $$\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{1/x}{-2/x^3}=\lim_{x\to0^+}-\frac{x^2}{2}=0.$$
rubricCriteria: Recognizes that the product must first be rewritten.
Verifies the infinite quotient and differentiates correctly.
Concludes that the limit is zero.

commonErrors.description: Applies L'Hospital's rule directly to the two factors.
commonErrors.consequence: The rule is used on a product rather than a quotient.

commonErrors.description: Treats $0\cdot(-\infty)$ as zero without analysis.
commonErrors.consequence: The indeterminate form is unresolved.

problems.flawedProof: The factor $x^2$ tends to zero, so it forces the product to zero regardless of the logarithm.

problems.title: The non-indeterminate logarithm trap
problems.objective: Reject an invalid L'Hospital application and evaluate the limit directly.
problems.statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{\log x}{x}$. Before computing, decide whether L'Hospital's rule applies and justify your decision.
problems.strategy: Classify the form before differentiating, substitute $t=1/x$, and compare the resulting negative product with $-t$.
hints: The quotient becomes $-t\log t$, which is at most $-t$ for large $t$.
problems.solution: L'Hospital's rule does not apply: the numerator tends to $-\infty$ while the denominator tends to $0^+$, so neither permitted indeterminate quotient occurs. Put $t=1/x$. Then $$\frac{\log x}{x}=-t\log t.$$ For $t\ge e$, $\log t\ge1$, hence $-t\log t\le-t$. Since $-t\to-\infty$, the comparison proves $$\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{\log x}{x}=-\infty.$$
rubricCriteria: Correctly classifies the limit as non-indeterminate for L'Hospital's rule.
Makes a valid substitution or equivalent direct comparison.
Proves that the limit is negative infinity.

commonErrors.description: Applies L'Hospital's rule because both numerator and denominator are unbounded or small in some sense.
commonErrors.consequence: The theorem's required forms are not satisfied.

commonErrors.description: Reports positive infinity after ignoring the sign of $\log x$.
commonErrors.consequence: The one-sided sign analysis is wrong.

problems.flawedProof: Differentiate numerator and denominator to get $1/x$, so the limit is positive infinity.

problems.title: A zero-over-zero limit the rule cannot prove
problems.objective: Show that a zero-over-zero form alone is insufficient when the derivative quotient has no limit.
problems.statement: Define $F(0)=0$ and $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)$ for $x\ne0$. Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{F(x)}x$ directly. Then prove that the derivative quotient $F'(x)/1$ has no limit as $x\to0$, so L'Hospital's rule cannot be used.
permittedResults: Sequential criterion for a limit and standard differentiation rules away from zero.
problems.strategy: Squeeze the original quotient, differentiate only on the punctured domain, and use two reciprocal-multiple-of-pi sequences.
problems.solution: For $x\ne0$, $$\left|\frac{F(x)}x\right|=|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|,$$ so the squeeze theorem gives the limit $0$. On the punctured domain, $$F'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x).$$ Along $x_n=(2\pi n)^{-1}$ this equals $-1$, while along $y_n=((2n+1)\pi)^{-1}$ it equals $1$. Both sequences tend to zero, so $F'(x)$ has no limit. The derivative-quotient hypothesis of L'Hospital's rule therefore fails even though the original $0/0$ limit exists.
rubricCriteria: Evaluates the original quotient by a squeeze bound.
Computes the punctured-domain derivative correctly.
Uses two sequences to show the derivative quotient has no limit and explains the theorem failure.

commonErrors.description: Concludes that every zero-over-zero form authorizes L'Hospital's rule.
commonErrors.consequence: The derivative-quotient limit hypothesis is omitted.

commonErrors.description: Differentiates $\sin(1/x)$ without the factor $-1/x^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The oscillatory derivative formula is wrong.

problems.flawedProof: The expression is zero over zero, so L'Hospital's rule applies automatically; differentiating gives zero.
problems.leanDraft:
import Mathlib

example (x : ℝ) : |x * Real.sin (1/x)| ≤ |x| := by
  calc
    |x * Real.sin (1/x)| = |x| * |Real.sin (1/x)| := abs_mul _ _
    _ ≤ |x| * 1 := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (abs_sin_le_one _) (abs_nonneg x)
    _ = |x| := by ring

problems.title: An infinity-over-infinity limit the rule cannot prove
problems.objective: Separate existence of an original quotient limit from convergence of its derivative quotient.
problems.statement: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{2x+\sin x}{x}$ directly. Then explain why L'Hospital's rule is unavailable even though the expression has the form $\infty/\infty$.
problems.strategy: Split the original quotient, bound its error, then compare the derivative quotient along even and odd multiples of pi.
hints: The error has absolute value at most $1/x$.
The derivative quotient is $2+\cos x$, which alternates along multiples of $\pi$.
problems.solution: We have $$\frac{2x+\sin x}{x}=2+\frac{\sin x}{x},$$ and $|\sin x/x|\le1/x\to0$, so the limit is $2$. The derivative quotient would be $2+\cos x$. Along $x_n=2\pi n$ it equals $3$, while along $y_n=(2n+1)\pi$ it equals $1$. Thus the derivative quotient has no limit, so L'Hospital's hypothesis fails. The original quotient still converges because the rule is sufficient, not a converse.
rubricCriteria: Evaluates the original quotient by a direct bound.
Shows the derivative quotient has two distinct subsequential limits.
Explains correctly that failure of L'Hospital's hypothesis does not imply divergence.

commonErrors.description: Claims the original quotient diverges because $2+\cos x$ diverges.
commonErrors.consequence: L'Hospital's rule is treated as a converse.

commonErrors.description: Claims infinity over infinity is itself an infinite value.
commonErrors.consequence: An indeterminate form is treated as arithmetic.

problems.flawedProof: Differentiate to get $2+\cos x$. Since that has no limit, the original quotient has no limit.
problems.leanDraft:
import Mathlib

example (x : ℝ) (hx : x ≠ 0) : |Real.sin x / x| ≤ 1 / |x| := by
  rw [abs_div]
  exact div_le_div_of_nonneg_right (abs_sin_le_one x) (abs_nonneg x)

problems.title: A classic exponential-sequence limit
problems.objective: Evaluate a standard variable-power limit with a logarithmic L'Hospital transformation.
problems.strategy: Take logarithms, rewrite the logarithmic product as a zero-over-zero quotient, and simplify its derivative quotient.
problems.solution: For $x>0$, set $y_x=(x/(x+1))^x$. Then $$\log y_x=\frac{\log(x/(x+1))}{1/x},$$ which has form $0/0$. Since $$\frac{d}{dx}\log\frac{x}{x+1}=\frac1x-\frac1{x+1}=\frac1{x(x+1)},$$ L'Hospital's rule gives $$\lim_{x\to\infty}\log y_x=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1/[x(x+1)]}{-1/x^2}=\lim_{x\to\infty}-\frac{x}{x+1}=-1.$$ Therefore $y_x\to e^{-1}$.
rubricCriteria: Introduces the logarithm and identifies the zero-over-zero quotient.
Differentiates and simplifies the logarithmic quotient correctly.
Exponentiates the limit and obtains $e^{-1}$.

commonErrors.consequence: The one-to-infinity form is not resolved.

commonErrors.description: Reports negative one as the original limit.
commonErrors.consequence: The logarithmic limit is not exponentiated.
